In the flickering light of state-sponsored newsreels, Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto and half his cabinet were captured performing the sacred rites of Hajj in Mecca. Draped in simple, unstitched white *ihram*, the political leadership engaged in vivid public displays of religious humility. Yet, this televised devotion was more than mere personal piety; it reflected a profound societal shift. Pakistan was increasingly turning its gaze westward toward the Arabian Peninsula, subtly submitting to the rising geopolitical, economic, and religious influence of the Gulf state.

That very year, this macro-level geopolitical alignment touched our family in a deeply personal way when Bhutto appointed my father to serve as the nation’s Hajj secretary. The reality of his high-profile assignment truly hit home during a routine trip to Melody Cinema. As we sat in the dark waiting for the main feature, the pre-show newsreel flickered onto the massive screen. To our utter astonishment, there was my father, towering alongside Prime Minister Bhutto in Mecca, bound together in the shared anonymity of their pilgrim robes. 

While the cinema audience witnessed a grand narrative of statecraft and public devotion, the true power of the pilgrimage unfolded in the quiet, inner life of our family. My mother was a woman afflicted by severe mysophobia, her daily existence dictated by an exacting fear of contamination and germs. Yet, the spiritual gravity of Mecca dismantled what years of domestic life could not. Humbled by the experience, she temporarily abandoned her lifelong anxieties, setting aside her extreme fear of dirt to sit directly on the bare, crowded ground during the rituals. In that sacred dust, the political and the personal collided, leaving an indelible mark on our family's memory.

By the mid-1970s, the geopolitical terrain of the Islamic world was undergoing a seismic realignment. Powered by the dizzying wealth of the oil boom, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia had begun to assert itself not merely as the custodian of the Holy Mosques, but as the financial and ideological vanguard of the region. In Islamabad, Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto—ever the astute, chameleon-like statesman—recognized that Pakistan’s economic and political survival required a profound public realignment toward Riyadh. To secure this alliance, Bhutto realized that secular rhetoric would no longer suffice; what was required was a grand, theatrical surrender of state ego to religious orthodoxy.

The instrument of this transformation was state-controlled media, specifically the newsreels that preceded every feature film in Pakistan’s bustling movie houses. Bhutto orchestrated a masterclass in political choreography. He led his entire cabinet, along with a cadre of newly elevated bureaucrats and military officials, on a high-profile pilgrimage to Mecca. 

The resulting newsreels were designed to break the illusion of political grandeur. Cameras captured the Prime Minister and his most formidable ministers—men usually seen in tailored Savile Row suits or crisp military starch—stripped of their worldly signifiers. Wrapped in the simple, unstitched white towels of the *ihram*, their bare feet caked with dusty sand, they were shown circumambulating the Kaaba, their faces glistening with sweat and devotion. The state broadcaster ensured these images were edited with a solemn, weightless reverie, presenting a government on its knees, humbled before the divine authority that Riyadh so effectively monopolized.

The true reach of this political theater, however, was felt far beyond the diplomatic corridors—it penetrated the quiet fabric of ordinary Pakistani households. 

I remember the evening my family witnessed one of these broadcasts. We were seated in the cool, velvet-upholstered dark of the Nishat Cinema, waiting for the evening’s Lollywood romance to begin. The projector whirred to life, illuminating suspended dust motes, and the state newsreel filled the screen. Beside me sat my mother, a woman whose life was governed by an exhausting, almost tyrannical fastidiousness. In our home, my mother’s devotion to order, cleanliness, and social decorum was absolute. She spent her days polishing brass, scolding servants for microscopic specks of dust, and maintaining a rigid hierarchy that kept the chaos of the outside world firmly beyond our front gate. To her, dignity was tied to immaculate presentation.

Yet, as the projector beamed the images of Mecca into the darkened theater, something broke in her posture. 

On the screen, a prominent federal minister—a man known in the press for his imperious swagger—was shown weeping openly, his hair shaved unevenly, jostled indiscriminately by thousands of ordinary worshippers. Then came Bhutto himself, walking bareheaded under the scorching Arabian sun, his eyes cast downward in profound, performative abjection. 

My mother stared, her hands frozen in her lap over her neatly pressed cotton sari. For a woman who viewed the slightest stain or loss of composure as a moral failing, watching the country's most powerful men willingly submit to dust, sweat, and total physical leveling was a revelation that seemed to bypass her intellectual defenses entirely. The state’s curated humility acted as a mirror, casting her own rigid perfectionism in a harsh, almost arrogant light. 

She let out a soft, trembling breath. For the rest of the newsreel, and indeed for long after we left the theater, the sharp, authoritative edge of her demeanor seemed blunted. The state had not just reshaped its foreign policy on that silver screen; it had successfully projected its manufactured piety directly into our family's private world, humbling the rulers of the nation and, in the very same stroke, taming the formidable spirit of my mother.

In the heart of the sacred city of **Mecca**, the noise of the worldly realm fades into a reverent hush. It is a place where millions gather not as kings, politicians, or commoners, but simply as human beings standing equal before the Divine. For any world leader, stepping into this vast ocean of faith is a profoundly **humbling** experience—a stark reminder of the impermanence of earthly power.

Consider the life of Benazir **Bhutto**, a figure whose name was synonymous with political charisma, high-stakes diplomacy, and the turbulent history of Pakistan. Born into political aristocracy and hardened by exile, tragedy, and the brutal realities of governance, she moved through a world of bulletproof convoys, state banquets, and fierce ideological battles. 

Yet, when Bhutto performed her pilgrimage to Mecca, the heavy armor of leadership fell away. 

Surrounded by the gleaming white marble of the Grand Mosque and the towering presence of the Kaaba, the grand narrative of political dynasties faded. In Mecca, there are no prime ministers or presidents. Clad in simple attire, walking shoulder-to-shoulder with millions of believers from every corner of the globe, Bhutto was stripped of her geopolitical weight. The overwhelming unity of the crowd—where a head of state prays alongside a humble farmer—serves as the ultimate equalizer.

For someone like Bhutto, whose life was constantly defined by the pursuit and defense of authority, the experience in Mecca offered a sacred reframing. It was a moment to acknowledge that all political power is fleeting, and that true strength lies in humility. The chanting of the pilgrims, the shared steps around the Kaaba, and the deep stillness of prayer provided a sanctuary of peace far removed from the storm of global politics.

Ultimately, the image of a leader like Bhutto in Mecca captures a universal truth. No matter how high one rises in the eyes of humanity, standing in that holy sanctuary is an undeniably **humbling** reminder of our shared frailty, our collective equality, and the quiet beauty of surrendering the ego to something far greater than ourselves.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a brief, evocative memoir snippet about growing up in Pakistan during Zulfikar Ali Bhutto's presidency, focusing on a memory of watching a state newsreel at Melody Cinema.
counterfactuals.output:
In the mid-seventies, Islamabad still smelled of wet pine and fresh cement, but inside Melody Cinema, the air was a thick, velvet brew of fried samosas, Capstan tobacco smoke, and quiet anticipation. I was nine years old, my knees pressed against the scratchy upholstery, waiting for the matinee. But before the main feature, the heavy curtains parted, and the projector’s beam sliced through the dark like a shaft of illuminated dust.

The state newsreel crackled to life, and suddenly he filled the screen: Zulfikar Ali Bhutto. 

The auditorium would settle into a reverent, charged silence. Bhutto didn’t move across the celluloid like other men; he surged. His collars were wide, his dark hair swept back, his hands slicing the air with theatrical precision as he addressed oceans of people waving green flags. *Roti, Kapra, Makaan*—the slogan felt less like politics and more like a fever dream of modern Pakistan, rebuilding itself from the heartbreak of 1971 with sheer, unyielding bravado. 

Beside me, my father would lean forward, his face caught in the flickering silver light of a leader who made an entire nation feel impossibly tall. Outside, the young city waited under the dark shadow of the Margalla Hills, but inside the glow of Melody Cinema, under Bhutto’s fierce, sweeping gaze, the future felt dangerously, magnificently bright.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a passage of literary non-fiction narrated by someone whose father was appointed Hajj secretary by Bhutto. Include details about seeing the cabinet in Mecca on screen, as well as the humorous humbling of the narrator's mysophobic mother.
counterfactuals.output:
In the sweltering autumn of 1974, when Zulfikar Ali Bhutto’s populist charisma still hung over Pakistan like a heady, intoxicating perfume, my father received a crisp, thick envelope sealed with the green crest of the State. Bhutto, in his grand effort to centralize and Islamicize the administrative machinery, had appointed my father as the Joint Secretary of Hajj. Overnight, our modest government quarter in Islamabad transformed into a shrine of logistical frenzy. My father, a man whose life had previously been governed by the quiet filing of agrarian land titles, was suddenly tasked with coordinating the soul’s ultimate journey for tens of thousands of countrymen.

Back then, history arrived in our living room through a boxy, wooden-framed PTV television that required five minutes to warm up, its glowing cathode screen humming like a hive of bees. It was on that screen that the surreal drama of the state unfolded. I remember the evening the live satellite broadcast from Makkah flickered into view. There, beneath the blinding glare of the Saudi sun, was the Pakistani cabinet. 

Back in Rawalpindi, these ministers were terrifying figures—men of heavy tweed, sharp moustaches, and imperial demeanors, who barked orders from behind mahogany desks. But on the screen, stripped of their tailoring and draped in the stark, unstitched white towels of the *ihram*, they looked astonishingly vulnerable. We watched, mesmerized, as the Minister of Fuel and Power, a man famous for his tyrannical temper, shuffled awkwardly near the Kaaba, his bare shoulders sunburned, looking less like a custodian of the republic and more like a bewildered ghost who had lost his luggage. Bhutto’s grand delegation had been thoroughly peeled of its bureaucratic plumage. They were just men, exposed and sweating, adrift in a sea of millions.

If the TV offered a lesson in political humility, our trip to the Holy Land offered an even greater theological comedy at the expense of my mother. 

My mother’s devotion to God was matched only by her profound, unyielding terror of microbes. She approached the physical world not as a divine creation, but as a biohazard zone waiting to infect her family. In Islamabad, her life was an endless campaign of carbolic soap, boiling water, and handkerchiefs pre-soaked in Dettol. To her, hell was not a pit of fire, but a public restroom.

When my father announced that we, too, would be accompanying the official delegation, my mother’s spiritual ecstasy was immediately undercut by a acute panic over public sanitation. She packed three trunks: one for clothes, and two entirely dedicated to antiseptics, surgical masks, sterile gauze, and custom-stitched canvas slipcovers for hotel furniture. 

The humbling of my mother began the moment we stepped onto the plain of Mina. 

Hajj is, by design, the ultimate equalizer—a divine assault on human pretension. For my mother, it was an assault on her very sanity. On the first night in the tent city, she attempted to establish a germ-free perimeter. She swept the desert sand with a whisk broom, laid down three layers of plastic sheeting, and forbade anyone from entering without wiping their feet with rubbing alcohol. 

By day two, the desert laughed at her. A sudden, light dust storm swept through the valley, coating everything—the carpets, the dates, her sacred Dettol bottles—in a fine, unstoppable layer of ancient Arabian silt. 

The climax of her undoing occurred in the courtyard of the Masjid al-Haram. It was fifty degrees Celsius. A crowd of half a million worshippers was moving in unison, a human tide of sweat, tears, and dust. My mother, wearing rubber gloves and a face mask, was attempting to navigate the Tawaf like a deep-sea diver avoiding contact with the water. 

Then, disaster struck. In the press of the crowd, her glove caught on a bystander’s sleeve and snapped off. In her shock, she stumbled, dropping her canvas bag. Out rolled her precious, last bottle of hand sanitizer. Before she could rescue it, a heavy-set pilgrim from Nigeria accidentally stepped on it, bursting the plastic and sending the fragrant, clear gel oozing into the sacred dust.

My mother froze. She looked at her bare hand. She looked at the floor, where her pristine white linen hem was now caked in the mud of a hundred thousand sweaty feet. A woman next to her, a villager from Sindh who had saved her entire life’s earnings for this week, reached out with a warm, damp, unabashedly unsterilized hand, grasped my mother’s bare palm, and smiled. 

"Brother's sister," the woman said softly in Sindhi, pointing toward the black cube of the Kaaba, "look up. We are here."

I watched my mother’s face. For three seconds, her brain waged a desperate war between a lifetime of mysophobia and the overwhelming, terrifying majesty of the moment. Then, something cracked. The tension left her shoulders. The hyper-vigilance drained from her eyes. 

She let go of the mask resting on her chin. She did not wipe her hand. With her fine clothes stained with Mina’s dust and her germ-free bubble violently popped, my mother took the Sindhi woman’s unwashed hand, squeezed it tightly, and wept.

Later that night, as we sat on the marble floor sipping Zamzam water from a shared plastic cup that had passed through at least four sets of hands, my father looked at her, his eyes twinkling with bureaucratic mischief. 

"Shall I fetch the Dettol, begum?" he whispered.

My mother took another sip of the holy water, wiped her mouth with the back of her dirty sleeve, and smiled. "Be quiet," she said, her voice lighter than I had ever heard it. "God is clean enough."
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a scene exploring how Pakistani political leaders in the 1970s used public acts of Islamic piety to align with Saudi Arabia, told through the personal, vivid recollection of a child seeing their parents on a cinema newsreel.
counterfactuals.output:
The year was 1974, and the air inside the Nishat Cinema smelled of stale cigarette smoke, damp velvet, and the sweet, heavy tang of fried samosas. I was nine years old, my knees wedged against the wooden seat in front of me, swinging my feet to the rhythmic hum of the massive ceiling fans overhead. 

We had come to see an American action film, but first came the *Department of Films and Publications* state newsreel. 

The silver screen flickered to life with a crackle of static, bathed in a beam of chalky white light that cut through the darkness over our heads. The martial trumpet fanfare sounded, announcing the news of the nation. But the music soon shifted, softening into solemn, devotional strings. 

"Lahore," the narrator’s baritone boomed in Urdu, crisp and authoritative. "*The Historic Islamic Summit.*"

On screen, the sun beat down on the red sandstone courtyard of the Badshahi Mosque. The camera panned over a sea of white caps and waving green flags. It was the moment Prime Minister Bhutto had engineered to reforge Pakistan’s identity after the heartbreak of 1971—turning our eyes away from the lost East, away from India, and toward the wealthy, oil-rich deserts of the Middle East.

Then came the grand procession. 

There was King Faisal of Saudi Arabia, tall, austere, and regal in his flowing dark *bisht* trimmed with gold thread. Beside him walked Prime Minister Bhutto, a man I was used to seeing on the front page of the newspaper wearing Western suits or his utilitarian *Awami* shirts. But on this day, the screen showed a different man. Bhutto wore a pristine black *sherwani* and a *Jinnah* cap, his hands folded devoutly in front of him, his face set in an expression of profound, almost performance-art humility. 

The camera cut to the collective Friday prayer. Thousands of men bowed in unison, a human wave of devotion. 

My heart jumped into my throat when the camera glided past the foreign dignitaries and focused on the row of Pakistani protocol officers and press aides standing just behind the royal Saudi delegation. 

"Look!" I gasped, grabbing the stiff sleeve of my father’s shirt in the dark. "Abba, look!"

My father shifted uncomfortably in his seat beside me, letting out a soft shush, though I saw the faint, embarrassed twitch of a smile at the corner of his mouth. 

There, illuminated on the thirty-foot screen, was my father. 

He was standing near the marble steps, dressed in a newly tailored black coat he had taken out a loan to buy. Beside him, tucked slightly into the shadow of the archway, was my mother. In our household, Ammi wore brightly colored chiffon *saris* and kept her shoulder-length hair tied loosely back. But on the newsreel, she was unrecognizable, draped in a heavy, brilliant-white *chadar* that covered her completely, leaving only her wide, cautious eyes visible. 

The camera caught my father as the call to prayer echoed through the speakers. On cue, alongside the politicians and diplomats, Abba raised his hands to his ears to begin the prayer. His gesture was exaggerated, solemn, almost panicked in its precision. He cast a quick, darting glance toward the Saudi delegation to ensure his posture mirrored theirs, his fingers cupping his ears in the exact manner favored by the Gulf scholars who had arrived in swarms that week.

In that flickering dark room, my nine-year-old mind felt a strange, chilling disconnect. 

At home, religion was a gentle, quiet thing—the smell of rosewater on Thursday evenings, my grandmother whispering verses over a bowl of water, Abba debating socialism with his friends over teacups filled with cheap local tea. But on the cinema screen, piety was loud, grand, and stiff. It was framed by Saudi petrodollars, giant green banners, and black-and-white cameras capturing every choreographed arc of prostration. 

Bhutto raised his hands in *dua*, his palms turned upward to the sky, flanked by the Saudi monarch. In the row behind them, my father raised his hands in the exact same vector, his eyes closed tightly, performing devoutness for the camera, for the State, and for the tall men in gold-trimmed robes who held the future of our economy in their pockets.

The newsreel cut to a shot of King Faisal waving to a cheering crowd as green confetti rained down like money from the sky, and then the film cut to black. The upbeat, brassy soundtrack of the feature film exploded from the speakers, and the audience around us began to chatter again.

I glanced sideways at my father in the dim theater light. He was staring straight ahead at the screen, sipping his lukewarm glass of orange soda, his posture slumped back into his usual relaxed, quiet self. The black *sherwani* was back in the wardrobe at home, wrapped in plastic to keep the moths away. 

"You looked very holy, Abba," I whispered.

My father turned to me, the blue light of the main feature reflecting in his eyes. He didn't laugh. He just offered a tired, knowing smile, patted my knee, and whispered back, "In this country, beta, when the wind blows from the desert, everyone learns how to bow."
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a prose excerpt contrasting a mother's extreme germaphobia at home with her sitting on the dusty ground during Hajj in a newsreel alongside Bhutto's political elite.
counterfactuals.output:
At home, my mother treated the universe outside our front door as a biological hazard. She ruled our house with a spray bottle of Dettol and a box of white cloth rags, her knuckles permanently red and raw from the harsh carbolic soap she forced upon us the second we stepped inside. To Ammi, a speck of street dust on the sofa was not merely dirt; it was a moral failing, a microscopic invasion. She would re-wash already-clean plates, recoil from the touch of paper currency, and scrub the brass doorknobs until they hummed with the sterile, chemical stench of a hospital ward.

Yet there she was, frozen in the flicker of a 1975 state newsreel reel, preserved on dusty 16mm film. 

In the broadcast, the PTV camera panned across the searing, sun-bleached plain of Arafat during the Hajj. The footage was grainy, but her face was unmistakable. She sat cross-legged directly on the pale, unwashed dirt of the desert, surrounded by the heavyweights of Zulfikar Ali Bhutto’s political court. To her left sat the polished, high-society wives of the Pakistan People’s Party cabinet—women who usually moved through air-conditioned drawing rooms in Karachi—their dark sunglasses reflecting the blinding Arabian sun. Just a few feet away, Bhutto’s diplomats in crisp white *ihrams* spoke in hushed, earnest tones, their political armor temporarily stripped down to simple cloth. 

And in the middle of this elite cosmos sat my mother, completely unbothered by the sacred chaos. Dust coated the hem of her white cotton chador; fine gray silt clung to the damp skin of her bare ankles. The woman who would boil a teacup twice before drinking from it was letting the hot desert wind blow grime directly into her face, resting her un-sanitized palms flat against the earth. On film, as the camera lingered on her face, there was no twitch of disgust, no compulsive reaching for a handkerchief. In the presence of the divine, surrounded by power and dust, the soil was no longer a germ to be eradicated—it was holy, and for the first time in her life, she was willing to let the world touch her.

Stepping out into the blinding twilight, the grand, alien silhouette of the Faisal Mosque loomed against the Margalla Hills like a marble fortress—a breathtaking gift that doubled as a shadow, reminding us that our culture, like the movies we were permitted to see, had been rewritten by the hand of a distant benefactor.
